summary: Describes generic threats to routing protocols. It covers threat sources and capabilities, actions and consequences, and the harm attacks can do to users or the network. This is informational background for protocol designers.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers pass directions around. This lists the ways a bad actor could give fake directions, and how much damage that could do.

questions: what are the threats to routing protocols
what are the types of threat consequences
subtitle: A vocabulary of who attacks routing protocols, what they do, and the damage that results.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols can be attacked in ways that harm individual users or the operation of a whole network, and there was no shared description of those threats.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out a protocol-independent threat model: threat sources and their capabilities, four kinds of consequence, and a list of recognizable threat actions such as spoofing, falsification and interference.
tldr.outcome: It is a precursor to a common set of security requirements for routing protocols, and it is protocol independent.

today: RFC 4593 is Informational, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a protocol-independent description of routing threats rather than a set of requirements.

sections.title: Why a Threat Model
sections.content:
RFC 4593 summarizes generic threats to routing protocols, including threat sources, threat actions and threat consequences, along with a breakdown of routing functions that can be attacked separately. It is meant as a precursor to developing a common set of security requirements for routing protocols.

The scope is attacks against robust, well-considered implementations of protocols such as OSPF (RFC 2328), IS-IS, RIP (RFC 2453) and BGP (RFC 4271). Bad or incomplete implementations, and attacks on implementation-specific weaknesses, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can build a lock, you need a list of the ways burglars get in. This document is that list for routers, not the lock itself.

sections.title: Routing Functions That Can Be Attacked
sections.content:
The RFC splits what routing protocols do into three shared functions, so that each can be considered separately.

  • Transport subsystem: sending messages to neighbors over an underlying protocol. OSPF uses IP, while other protocols may run over TCP.
  • Neighbor state maintenance: forming and keeping neighbor relationships, which is the first step of topology determination, for example through Hello exchanges in OSPF.
  • Database maintenance: exchanging topology and reachability information and collecting it in routing databases.

Some messages control the state of the protocol, such as neighbor maintenance messages. Others carry the information used for forwarding, such as database updates.
sections.plainLanguage: A router has three jobs: talk to its neighbors, remember who its neighbors are, and keep a map. A trickster can mess with any one of them.

sections.title: Threat Sources: Outsiders and Byzantine Routers
sections.content:
A threat source, for deliberate attack, is a motivated and capable adversary. The most common goal assumed is to make inter-domain routing malfunction, so that traffic follows a path other than the one a healthy protocol would compute. That can allow passive wiretapping or active man-in-the-middle attacks, including discarding traffic. Other motives include financial gain related to traffic volume, and damage to the network infrastructure, for example by causing excessive UPDATE messages.

The capabilities range upward. All adversaries are presumed able to direct packets at routers and spoof the IP source address. Some can monitor links and replay or mimic routing traffic. Some can mount man-in-the-middle attacks on a link. Some can subvert routers or the management workstations that control them, which the RFC calls Byzantine failures, the most serious form. The RFC therefore groups sources into two kinds: outsiders, who are not legitimate participants in the routing protocol, and Byzantine routers, which are faulty, misconfigured or subverted legitimate participants. Cryptanalytic attacks are ignored, because the RFC assumes any cryptographic countermeasures use algorithms resistant to attack.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of troublemakers: strangers shouting from outside, and a router that is part of the group but has gone bad, like a classmate who starts passing around false notes.

sections.title: Four Kinds of Consequence
sections.content:
Following the Internet Security Glossary (RFC 2828), a threat consequence is a security violation resulting from a threat action. There are four types.

  • Disclosure: an attacker gets routing information without authorization. The RFC notes that confidentiality is not generally a design goal of routing protocols.
  • Deception: a legitimate router accepts a forged routing message as authentic.
  • Disruption: a legitimate router's operation is interrupted or prevented.
  • Usurpation: an attacker takes control of services a legitimate router provides to others.

One action can cause several consequences. In the RFC's dual-homed example, Network 1 is reached through Router A and Router B, and Router A is preferred. If a compromised Router B advertises a better metric, devices on the Internet choose B. Routers using B are deceived, and Router A is usurped.

Damage is also described by scope. Network-wide effects include congestion, blackholes, looping, partition, churn, instability, overcontrol and clog. Effects on a particular host or network include starvation, eavesdrop, cut, delay and looping. A consequence zone is the area affected, from a single link or router up to the global Internet, and a consequence period is the time affected, which can outlast the attack. The RFC cites an original ARPANET link-state error that kept flooding until the entire network was power cycled.
sections.plainLanguage: Trouble comes in four flavors: peeking at secrets, fooling someone, stopping someone from working, or sneaking into their job. One bad act can do more than one at once.

sections.title: Recognizable Threat Actions
sections.content:
Section 4 names actions that are not tied to one protocol. Deliberate exposure, sniffing and traffic analysis all lead to disclosure of routing information. Spoofing means an illegitimate device assumes a legitimate one's identity. It is rarely the true attack, but it enables others, and it can also stand alone, for example to form a neighbor relationship that denies the real router.

Falsification is sending false routing information, which only an originator or a forwarder can do. Originators can overclaim, advertising control of resources they do not have or are not authorized to advertise, or misclaim, advertising resources they do control in a way the administrator did not intend, such as wrong link costs in an OSPF LSA. Forwarders can misstate attributes. In RIP the hop count should rise by 1, and an attacker might raise it by two; in BGP an attacker might delete AS numbers from the AS PATH. They can also delete, insert or substitute data, or replay outdated data.

Interference inhibits exchanges between legitimate routers, for example with noise, dropped or delayed packets, or breaking synchronization. Overload places excess burden on routers, for example by triggering an excessive amount of state.
sections.plainLanguage: The tricks include listening in, pretending to be someone else, giving wrong directions, getting in the way, and flooding a router with too much work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the whole document is security related. It notes that routing protocols have largely remained unprotected and open to malicious attacks, discusses known inter- and intra-domain threats, and lays the foundation for other documents on security requirements. It is protocol independent.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole document is about keeping routers safe, because today most of them trust each other too easily.

items.label: Deliberate exposure
items.desc: A controlled router releases routing information to those who should not have it.

items.label: Traffic analysis
items.desc: Learning from the characteristics of data traffic on a subverted link.

items.label: Spoofing
items.desc: An illegitimate device assumes a legitimate identity.

items.label: Falsification
items.desc: Sending false routing information as an originator or forwarder.

items.label: Overload
items.desc: Placing excess burden on legitimate routers.
